docs.title: Value at Risk
docs.text:
Imagine managing a portfolio worth $10 million. Before the next trading day, you want a practical answer to this question:

How large could tomorrow's loss be before it falls into the worst 5% of outcomes in our model?

Value at Risk (VaR) gives that dividing line. If the portfolio's one-day 95% VaR is $1 million, the model assigns a 95% probability to a loss of $1 million or less and a 5% probability to a larger loss. The estimate depends on today's positions, the available information, and the model's assumptions 1.

VaR is not a maximum possible loss

Losses beyond VaR can be much larger. A 95% confidence level does not mean that the portfolio is safe 95% of the time, that the estimate is 95% certain to be correct, or that losses stop at the VaR threshold.

docs.title: How to read VaR
docs.text:
Every VaR report needs three ingredients:

Ingredient Example What it tells you Loss amount $1 million The estimated loss threshold, not a loss limit Horizon One trading day How far ahead the forecast looks Confidence level 95% The model probability of not exceeding the threshold

A useful way to picture 95% VaR is to imagine 100 equally likely model scenarios. Roughly 95 produce losses at or below the threshold, and roughly five produce larger losses. This is an explanation of probability, not a promise that every block of 100 trading days will contain exactly five exceptions.

docs.title: A picture of the threshold
docs.text:
The horizontal axis shows profit and loss (P&L). Negative values on the left are losses, and positive values on the right are gains. The dashed line is at \(-\$1\) million, the P&L cutoff corresponding to a reported VaR of \(+\$1\) million. The hatched region to its left represents losses larger than $1 million. Probability is represented by area under the curve, not by the curve's height at a single point.

This smooth bell curve is an illustration, not a claim that actual P&L follows a normal distribution. It uses a zero-mean normal P&L model with a standard deviation of approximately $607,957, chosen so that its 5th percentile is \(-\$1\) million. The left tail continues beyond the drawing. Actual portfolios can have much heavier tails.

The figure is a local SVG generated with Matplotlib. MkDocs displays it as an ordinary image, so readers do not download a plotting library or need JavaScript to see it.

docs.title: What the mathematics says
docs.text:
Readers who only need the interpretation can continue to the estimation methods. This section makes the conventions explicit for implementation.

Let \(V_0\) be today's portfolio value and \(V_h\) its value at the end of a horizon \(h\). For a portfolio with fixed positions and no intermediate cash flows, define loss as:

\[ L_h = V_0 - V_h. \]

A positive \(L_h\) means a loss. A negative \(L_h\) means a gain. In production, specify how coupons, dividends, funding, fees, and position changes enter profit and loss rather than silently mixing definitions.

The plot uses the opposite axis convention: profit and loss is \(\Pi_h=V_h-V_0=-L_h\). For a continuous distribution with a unique quantile, the left-tail P&L cutoff is:

\[ q_{1-c}(\Pi_h)=-\operatorname{VaR}_c(L_h). \]

Thus the same risk can be shown as a negative cutoff on a P&L plot or a positive quantile of losses. We report the monetary VaR, not its negative P&L cutoff. For discrete distributions, specify quantile endpoint conventions before applying this sign reversal, because probability masses can make lower-quantile identities fail at a boundary.

Write \(c\) for the confidence level and \(\alpha=1-c\) for the tail probability. Throughout this article, the subscript on VaR is the confidence level. Thus \(\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}\) means 95% VaR, not a 95% tail probability.

\[ \operatorname{VaR}_{c}(L_h) = \inf\{x\in\mathbb{R}:\Pr(L_h\leq x)\geq c\}. \]

This is the \(c\)-quantile of losses: the smallest threshold whose cumulative probability reaches the confidence level. All probabilities are forecasts conditional on the information available when the estimate is made.

For a continuous distribution, the probability of a loss strictly above the quantile is \(1-c\). For a distribution with probability concentrated at particular values, that probability can be smaller. VaR can also be negative if even the chosen quantile is a gain. Some reports floor it at zero, but that is an additional reporting convention.

docs.title: Choosing confidence and horizon
docs.text:
Common reporting levels include 95% and 99%. For the same loss distribution, a higher confidence level cannot give a lower VaR. It also moves the estimate into a part of the distribution where data are scarcer. Raising the confidence level does not make the underlying model more reliable.

A one-day horizon is useful for daily monitoring. Longer horizons may suit positions that take longer to unwind. Always compare like with like: a one-day 95% VaR and a ten-day 99% VaR answer different questions. Regulatory requirements also depend on the applicable framework and jurisdiction, as discussed below.

docs.title: Three ways to estimate VaR
docs.text: All three methods follow the same basic idea: construct plausible portfolio losses and locate the chosen quantile. They differ in how those losses are produced.

docs.title: Historical simulation: replay past market moves
docs.text:
Historical simulation asks: What would today's portfolio lose if past market moves happened again?

  1. Keep today's positions fixed.
  2. Collect historical changes in relevant prices, interest rates, exchange rates, and other risk factors.
  3. Apply each day's joint changes to today's market levels and revalue the portfolio.
  4. Sort the resulting losses from smallest to largest.

Replaying joint changes preserves the relationships observed on those historical dates. Repricing today's positions is important. Simply using the portfolio's old realized profit and loss can mix different holdings and trading decisions 1.

For \(n\) equally weighted scenarios, write the ordered losses as \(L_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq L_{(n)}\). Using the empirical inverse-distribution convention:

\[ k=\lceil cn\rceil,\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{VaR}}_c=L_{(k)}. \]

With 250 scenarios and 95% confidence, \(k=\lceil0.95\times250\rceil=238\). Take the 238th smallest loss, which is also the 13th largest loss. Twelve scenarios lie strictly above it if there are no ties.

For a fixed, positive investment \(V_0\) with simple returns \(r_i\) and no cash flows, \(L_i=-V_0r_i\). If returns are sorted from worst to best, the equivalent formula is:

\[ \widehat{\operatorname{VaR}}_c =-V_0r_{(n-\lceil cn\rceil+1)}. \]

In the 250-scenario example, this uses the 13th worst return. If that return is \(-2\%\) and \(V_0=\$10\) million, the monetary VaR is $200,000. Without the factor \(V_0\), the result is a return-based measure, not a dollar amount.

Quantile conventions affect the result

Software may interpolate between observations instead of selecting a single order statistic. State the convention explicitly. For example, with 100 distinct scenarios and 95% confidence, the rule above selects the 95th smallest loss, or the sixth largest. A different rounding rule need not give the same answer.

Historical simulation does not require a normal distribution. It can reflect skewness and extreme losses present in the chosen sample, but it cannot invent crises absent from that sample. Equally weighting observations also gives an old calm day the same weight as a recent volatile day. Longer histories supply more tail observations but may mix market regimes that no longer resemble today's conditions.

docs.title: Parametric VaR: use a distributional model
docs.text:
A simple parametric model assumes that the portfolio's return is approximately normal. Instead of replaying every date, it summarizes risk through an expected return, volatility, and correlations.

For a linear portfolio, let \(\mathbf{w}\) contain position values divided by a fixed positive reference value \(V_0\). Let \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) be the mean vector and covariance matrix of risk-factor simple returns over the chosen horizon. Then:

\[ \mu_p=\mathbf{w}^{T}\boldsymbol{\mu},\qquad \sigma_p=\sqrt{\mathbf{w}^{T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}}, \] \[ \operatorname{VaR}_c =V_0\left(z_c\sigma_p-\mu_p\right), \qquad z_c=\Phi^{-1}(c). \]

Here \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the standard normal quantile function. At 95% confidence, \(z_{0.95}\approx1.645\). Both \(\sigma_p\) and \(\mu_p\) are expressed as returns, and multiplying by \(V_0\) converts the result to money. For derivatives, a delta-normal model uses linearized risk-factor exposures instead of treating option values as linear investments.

Example. A $10 million linear portfolio has daily volatility of 1% and assumed mean return of zero. Its one-day 95% VaR is approximately:

\[ \$10{,}000{,}000\times1.645\times0.01 =\$164{,}500. \]

This method is fast and useful as a benchmark. Its weaknesses are the distributional assumption, estimated correlations, and any linear approximation. Heavy tails can make a normal model understate extreme losses. Options can respond nonlinearly to price and volatility changes, so a delta-only approximation can miss important gains or losses.

docs.title: When can we scale by the square root of time?
docs.text:
If daily monetary losses are independent and identically distributed normal variables, with mean \(\mu_L\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_L\), their sum over \(h\) days satisfies:

\[ \operatorname{VaR}_{c,h} =h\mu_L+z_c\sigma_L\sqrt{h}. \]

The shortcut \(\operatorname{VaR}_{c,h}=\sqrt{h}\operatorname{VaR}_{c,1}\) follows only when the mean is zero under these assumptions. Independence and finite variance alone explain how variance scales, not how an arbitrary tail quantile scales.

Compounded returns, changing positions, volatility clustering, illiquidity, jumps, and nonlinear payoffs can invalidate the shortcut. When these effects matter, model the target horizon directly.

docs.title: Monte Carlo simulation: generate model scenarios
docs.text:
Monte Carlo simulation asks: What losses arise from many hypothetical market moves generated by a chosen model?

Specify how risk factors evolve and depend on one another, simulate their future values or paths, and revalue the portfolio in each scenario. Sort the resulting losses and apply the same quantile convention used for historical simulation 2.

Full revaluation can capture option curvature and path-dependent payoffs more faithfully than a linear approximation. But simulation is not automatically accurate. Its results still depend on the risk-factor model, parameter estimates, dependence assumptions, and pricing models.

Distinguish the real-world probabilities used to forecast market moves from the risk-neutral valuation models used to price derivatives within each scenario. A pricing model alone does not supply a real-world loss forecast.

Tail estimates also need enough simulations. At 99% confidence, only about 100 of 10,000 scenarios are expected to lie beyond the true quantile. Use convergence checks and quantify simulation uncertainty rather than assuming that a large-looking scenario count is sufficient.

docs.title: Loss severity beyond the threshold
docs.text:
Two portfolios can have the same 99% VaR of $1 million, even if one has losses just above $1 million in the tail while the other can lose $20 million. VaR identifies the entrance to the tail, not what happens inside it.

Expected Shortfall (ES) addresses this missing dimension by averaging the worst fraction \(1-c\) of outcomes. A definition that also handles discrete distributions is:

\[ \operatorname{ES}_c(L) =\frac{1}{1-c}\int_c^1\operatorname{VaR}_u(L)\,du. \]

For a continuous distribution with no probability mass at the threshold, this equals the expected loss conditional on exceeding VaR. With discrete scenarios or ties, simply averaging losses strictly above VaR need not give the correctly weighted ES. ES still depends on the model and should be accompanied by stress tests.

docs.title: Diversification is not always reflected consistently
docs.text:
A risk measure is subadditive if the measured risk of combined losses is no greater than the sum of the separately measured risks:

\[ \operatorname{VaR}_c(X+Y) \leq\operatorname{VaR}_c(X)+\operatorname{VaR}_c(Y). \]

VaR does not always satisfy this inequality. A simple example shows why:

  • Investment A loses $100 with probability 4% and otherwise loses nothing.
  • Investment B has the same loss distribution, independently of A.
  • Each investment's 95% VaR is zero because its probability of no loss is 96%.
  • Together, the probability of at least one loss is \(1-0.96^2=7.84\%\). The combined 95% VaR is therefore $100, which exceeds the sum of the individual VaRs.

This does not mean that diversification always fails or that VaR always violates subadditivity. It shows how separate quantile thresholds can hide rare losses. ES is subadditive for integrable losses, which is one reason it complements VaR 1.

docs.title: Model uncertainty and market stress
docs.text:
Historical, normal, and Monte Carlo models can give different answers for the same portfolio. Investigate those differences rather than choosing whichever estimate is lowest.

A model fitted to a calm period may miss sudden volatility increases, broken correlations, or the cost of exiting positions in stressed markets. Add stress scenarios, liquidity analysis, sensitivity measures, and concentration limits. A statistical threshold is not a complete risk-management system.

docs.title: Count exceptions without using future information
docs.text:
An exception occurs when the realized loss exceeds the VaR forecast made before that loss was observed. For a daily backtest, record:

\[ I_t=\mathbf{1}\{L_t>\widehat{\operatorname{VaR}}_{c,t\mid t-1}\}, \qquad \widehat{p}=\frac{x}{N}, \qquad x=\sum_{t=1}^{N}I_t. \]

The notation \(t\mid t-1\) means that the forecast for day \(t\) uses information available by day \(t-1\). Do not recalibrate the historical forecast with data that arrived later.

For a correctly calibrated continuous 95% model, the expected exception rate is 5%. Over 250 days, the expected count is 12.5, but the realized count will be an integer and will vary. One exception does not prove failure, and no exceptions do not prove accuracy.

Compare forecasts with a consistent definition of profit and loss. A fixed-position VaR is naturally checked against hypothetical profit and loss on those positions. Actual trading profit and loss can also reflect intraday trades, fees, and other effects. Regulatory backtesting specifies its own comparisons.

docs.title: Check both frequency and clustering
docs.text:
The Kupiec unconditional coverage test asks whether the exception frequency is consistent with the target \(p=1-c\). Under an independent Bernoulli exception model:

\[ LR_{\mathrm{uc}} =-2\log\left( \frac{(1-p)^{N-x}p^x} {(1-\widehat{p})^{N-x}\widehat{p}^{\,x}} \right). \]

Under the null hypothesis and standard large-sample conditions, this statistic has an approximate \(\chi^2_1\) distribution. At \(x=0\) or \(x=N\), evaluate the likelihood by its limit, conventionally taking \(0^0=1\) here. Small tail samples can make the asymptotic approximation unreliable, so an exact binomial test is a useful alternative under the same independence assumption.

The count alone does not reveal whether exceptions cluster. Five exceptions spread across a year tell a different story from five in one week. Christoffersen's conditional coverage test combines coverage and independence checks 1.

Non-overlapping forecasts are easiest to interpret. Overlapping multi-day losses share observations and can create dependence even when the underlying daily model is correct. Passing a backtest is evidence about calibration, not proof that every model assumption is sound.

docs.title: Regulatory context
docs.text:
Separate legacy VaR capital rules from the revised market-risk framework. Older Basel internal-model rules used 99% ten-day VaR alongside stressed VaR and other charges. Presenting that arrangement as the universal current Basel requirement is misleading.

Under the Basel Committee's revised market-risk framework, often called the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB), the internal-model capital measure for modellable risk factors uses 97.5% Expected Shortfall, calibrated to stress and adjusted for prescribed liquidity horizons. The base horizon is ten days, with longer liquidity horizons for relevant risk factors. See the official Basel Framework, MAR33.

VaR still has a role in model backtesting. MAR32 specifies one-day VaR comparisons, including 99% bank-wide backtesting and 97.5% and 99% trading-desk tests.

Implementation dates and legal requirements vary by jurisdiction. The Basel standard is not a substitute for applicable local rules. Operational-risk capital is a separate risk category, and the regulatory output floor should not be described as a simple rule requiring every market-risk capital result to equal the higher of its internal-model and standardized estimates.

docs.title: How does a position change the total?
docs.text:
Incremental VaR compares a portfolio with and without a position:

\[ \operatorname{IVaR}_i =\operatorname{VaR}_c(\text{portfolio with position }i) -\operatorname{VaR}_c(\text{portfolio without position }i). \]

Keep the horizon, model, and other holdings consistent. A negative value means the position reduces measured VaR, as a hedge might do. It does not mean the position is risk-free.

Component VaR allocates total VaR using sensitivities to position amounts \(a_i\):

\[ C_i=a_i\frac{\partial\operatorname{VaR}_c(\mathbf{a})}{\partial a_i}. \]

If VaR is differentiable and positively homogeneous of degree one in those amounts, Euler's theorem gives \(\sum_i C_i=\operatorname{VaR}_c(\mathbf{a})\). These conditions matter. Empirical quantiles can be nonsmooth, and finite-difference allocations need not add up exactly. Component VaR is not the same as removing a whole position, and the abbreviation CVaR is best avoided here because it is also used for Conditional VaR.

docs.title: A practical reporting checklist
docs.text:
1. State the portfolio, valuation time, currency, horizon, and confidence level.
  2. Specify the model, data window, loss definition, and quantile convention.
  3. Validate positions, market data, and valuation inputs before calculation.
  4. Report VaR alongside ES, stress losses, sensitivities, and concentrations.
  5. Compare forecasts with limits and investigate breaches.
  6. Archive forecasts before outcomes occur, then backtest and review exceptions.
  7. Communicate uncertainty and model changes, not just a single number.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
VaR is a model-based loss threshold over a stated horizon at a stated confidence level. It is not a worst-case loss or a guarantee.

For a non-technical reader, the key follow-up questions are: What assumptions produced the number? How bad could losses beyond it become? And how well have previous forecasts performed?

docs.title: Statistics And Probability
docs.text:
This section is my go-to reference for essential probability and statistics concepts, that act as the building blocks that underpin everything from risk modeling to machine learning.

Think of this as a personal binacle where we dig into the "why" behind commonly-used equivalences and definitions. Instead of just accepting formulas at face value, we'll explore their origins and derivations. Whether you're developing a new model, validating assumptions, or simply need a quick refresher on the math that matters, you'll find it here.

We're covering the core stuff: distributions, expected values, moments, convergence theorems, and those elegant mathematical relationships that make quantitative work possible. Clear, rigorous, and ready for real-world application.

docs.title: Statistics vs Probability - Two Sides of the Same Coin
docs.text:
While often used interchangeably, statistics and probability are fundamentally different disciplines that approach uncertainty from opposite directions. Understanding their distinction is essential for rigorous quantitative work.

Probability is the mathematical framework for modeling uncertainty. It starts with a known model (a distribution, parameters, or generating process) and derives what outcomes we should expect. It's deductive reasoning: given the rules of the game, what will happen?

Statistics, on the other hand, works backward. It starts with observed data and attempts to infer the underlying model, parameters, or process that generated it. It's inductive reasoning: given what happened, what are the rules of the game?

Aspect Probability Statistics Direction Model → Data Data → Model Reasoning Deductive Inductive Starting Point Known distribution/parameters Observed samples Goal Predict outcomes Infer underlying process Example Question "If I flip a fair coin 100 times, what's the probability of getting exactly 60 heads?" "I flipped a coin 100 times and got 60 heads. Is the coin fair?" Tools Random variables, distributions, limit theorems Estimation, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals Uncertainty Source Randomness in future events Uncertainty about model parameters

docs.title: How They Complement Each Other
docs.text:
These two disciplines form a complete cycle in quantitative analysis:

  1. Probability provides the foundation: Statistical methods rely on probability theory to quantify uncertainty. When we construct confidence intervals or perform hypothesis tests, we use probabilistic calculations to assess how likely our observations are under various models.

  2. Statistics validates probability models: Real-world applications require us to choose appropriate probability models. Statistics gives us tools to test whether our probabilistic assumptions match observed data, estimate unknown parameters, and refine our models.

  3. Iteration drives insight: In practice, we move back and forth: propose a probabilistic model, use statistics to estimate its parameters and test its fit, refine the model based on diagnostics, and repeat. This iterative process is central to risk modeling, machine learning, and quantitative finance.

  4. Both handle uncertainty rigorously: Together, they provide a complete framework for reasoning under uncertainty. Thereby, probability tells us what to expect from known models, while statistics tells us which models are consistent with reality.

In this section, we'll explore both perspectives: the probabilistic foundations that define the rules, and the statistical techniques that let us learn those rules from data.

docs.title: Core Philosophy

Probability answers the question: "Given a known model or process, what outcomes should we expect?"

Starting from axioms and probability distributions, we build a rigorous mathematical structure that lets us: - Quantify uncertainty in future events - Derive properties of random variables - Establish limit theorems and convergence results - Model stochastic processes and information flow over time
